3. The suit was then contested mainly by defendant No. 3 taking the defence that the goods in question were not landed into their custody and that the suit was barred by limitation under section 109(2) of the Chittagong Port Act as it was not filed within a period of six months from the accrual of right to sue. But the trial court on consideration of evidence decreed the suit against defendant No. 3 holding, among other things, that the suit was not barred by limitation. This judgment and decree of the trial court was challenged in appeal but the appeal was dismissed by the High Court Divisional by the impugned judgment and decree dated March 5, 1980. 

 4. Leave was grants to consider whether the High Court Division correctly construed the relevant provisions of law, particularly sections 50A, 50B and 109 of the Chittagong Port Act. The main questions for decision are what is the law of limitation applicable to this case and what is the starting point of the limitation. Contention of the defendant althrough is that special law of limitation as prescribed in section 109(2) of the Chittagong Port Act is applicable to this case and that this period would start from 23.10.63, when the discharge of the goods from the vessel was completed or from 16.1.64 when the Short Landing Certificate was issued. Whereas the High Court Division held that section 109(2) does not lay down any special law of limitation and that the suit is governed by general law of limitation, namely, Article 115 of the Limitation Act which prescribes three years period of limitation starting after the expiration of one month after a notice of the suit is served upon the defendant Port Trust under section 109 (1) of the said Act, that is, from 9.2.65. Alternatively, the High Court Division held that even if the special limitation of six months is applicable still the suit will not be barred by limitation which would start from 20.11.64, the date on which the plaintiff got definite information that defendant No. 3 was responsible for the non-delivery. 

 7. Mr. Mozammel Huq, learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-appellant contends that the suit is barred by limitation under section 109(2) of the Chittagong Port Act which prescribes a period of six months for filing a suit against the Port Trust and that this section lays down a special limitation which is applicable to this suit. In support of this contention he has relied upon a decision of the High Court Division is Tajor Rahman v. Trustees of the Port of Chittagong, (1) where it has been held that section 109(2) of the Chittagong Port Act has prescribed a special period of limitation of six months for a suit against the Port Trust. This decision was given by a Division Bench. But the High Court Division in the instant case has obi served that "the previous decision can hardly be taken to be a precedent". The decision of one Division Bench is binding upon another Division Bench, but if the latter finds difficulty to agree with the previous decision, it is to refer the question to a larger Bench. This has not been done in this case. 

 8. In this case the High Court Division has held that section 109(2) does not lay down a special period of limitation for a suit against the Chittagong Port Trust for any-thing purportedly done under this Act, that "general law of limitation is not affected by section 109(2)" and that" Article 115 of the Limitation Act will apply to this suit" against the Port Trust. Article 115 of the Limitation Act, it may be kept in mind, prescribes a period of three years for a suit for compensation for the breach of any contract, expressed or implied. We find difficult to accept the view that section 109(2) does not lay down any special law of limitation. The Chittagong Port Act is itself a special statute relating to functions and activities of the Chittagong Port Trust only. Sub-section (1) of section 109 of this Act provides for filing a suit against the Board of Trustees, or any Trustee or any of the officers or servants of the Board for anything purporting to be done under this Act. A suit filed against any other person or authority such as defendants Nos. 1 and 2 is outside the ambit of this section. Section 109(2) prescribes a period of limitation for a suit filed only against the Port Trust of their officers and servants. This section is therefore a special law of limitation within the meaning of section 29 of the Limitation Act, and in terms of that section in a suit filed against the Port Trust or its officers or servants this law shall apply as if such period were prescribed therefor in the schedule of the Limitation Act. The views taken by the High Court Division that section 109(2) of the Chittagong Port Act is not a special law of limitation or that it does not affect the general law of limitation and Article 115 of the Limitation Act is applicable in this suit are not sustainable in law. This suit being a suit against the Chittagong Port Trust for anything purporting to be done under this Act is governed by section 109(2) and according to this section a suit if not filed within a period of six months from the accrual of the right to sue shall be dismissed, the provision for condo nation of delay under the. Limitation Act not being applicable to a case governed by this special law. 

 10. In the instant case the earliest point of time at which the plaintiff was in a position to put up his claim against the Port trust in November 20, 1964 when the plaintiff got the definite information that the Port Trust had received into its custody the missing goods. The Port Trust issued the Short Landing Certificate on 16-1-64 but this date cannot be the last point of limitation for a suit against the Port Trust which by this Certificate absolved itself of the responsibility for the goods and shifted the responsibility upon the carrier and his agent. On the basis of this Short Landing Certificate plaintiff filed the suit at the first instance against the carrier and his agent defendants No. 1 and 2. But after further enquiry defendants Nos. 1 and 2 ascertained that the missing drums were landed from the vessel and given into the care and custody of the Port Trust and accordingly they, by their letter dated 20-11-64, Ext. 10 (k) informed the plaintiff that the Port Trust was solely responsible for the shortage and in support of this claim they also produced convincing evidence. It is on that date that the plaintiff got definite knowledge that the Port Trust was responsible for the shortage and Port Trust's failure to deliver the cargo and as such cause of action against the Port Trust accrued on that date. 

 11. On a similar question the West Pakistan High Court in the case of 'Hail Adam vs. Levant Line' (1) took the same view. In that case the suit was brought first against the carrier and his agent for the short delivery of certain goods, but in the course of the evidence an officer of the Karachi Port Trust admitted that they had received the goods into custody. Upon this admission the Karachi Port Trust was impleaded as a defendant. By that time several years had passed since the landing of the goods and the issuing of the Short Landing Certificate. Contention was raised that the suit against the Port Trust was hopelessly barred by limitation as it was not filed within six months from the date of the Short Landing Certificate. The contention was rejected and it was held that it was not until the admission of the officer of the Port Trust revealing the definite knowledge that the cause of action arose. It was, therefore, held that "in such cases the test laid down is to find out when the plain-tiff could first have maintained his action to a successful result." 

 12. Sub-section (1) of section 109, however, provides that no suit shall be brought against the Port Trust until the expiration of one month next after a notice of the suit is served upon the Port Trust and that the court shall dismiss the suit unless such notice is proved. The High Court Division, in view of this mandatory provision as to notice, held that since non-compliance with this provision will result in "automatic, mandatory" dismissal of the suit, it cannot be said that the right to sue has accrued to the plaintiff unless this period of one month expires from the time of compliance with this mandatory provision. The provision as to prior notice for filing a suit is a matter of procedure intended to give the Port Trust an opportunity to tender sufficient amends before the suit is brought, as clearly provided in sub-section (3) of this section, whereas "right to sue" is a substantive right which accrues on the doing or omission to do certain things. So, the plaintiff will be entitled to add the notice period under sub-section (1) to the period of limitation prescribed under sub-section (2) and a reading of the two sub-sections together indicates to that affect. We are, therefore, of the view that right to sue in this case accrued on 20-11-64 which is the starting point of limitation in the suit against the Post Trust and that counting from this date the suit is found well within the period of limitation including the notice period.
